claims.text: An Eventhouse is a workspace-level container that can host multiple KQL databases, allowing them to share underlying capacity and resources so that cost and performance are jointly optimized across all contained databases.

Eventhouse monitoring is surfaced at the container level: a single system-overview page tracks storage, compute, ingestion rates, and top-queried databases across every KQL database inside the eventhouse, whereas individual KQL databases expose their own narrower metrics.

Sharing an Eventhouse link propagates the sender's permission level across all child items — KQL databases, tables, dashboards, functions, materialized views, and embedded querysets — whereas sharing an individual KQL database grants access only to that database and excludes Eventhouse-level navigation such as the system overview or the database list.

Eventhouse capacity consumption is metered through an 'UpTime' metric: CU seconds consumed equal the number of active seconds multiplied by the virtual core count allocated by the autoscaler to that eventhouse. When a KQL database is a child item of an eventhouse, its UpTime rolls up to the eventhouse item and no separate CU line appears for the database subitem.

KQL database storage is split into two independently billed tiers: a premium cache tier (comparable to ADLS premium) that holds the hot dataset governed by the caching policy, and a standard tier (comparable to ADLS hot) that holds the full retention window governed by the retention policy. Configuring a shorter cache window reduces premium-tier spend without affecting total queryable history.

When query demand exceeds capacity, an Eventhouse applies throttling in three escalating stages: proactive (queries slowed, ingestion unaffected), reactive (both queries and ingestion paused but no data lost), and extreme-reactive (ingestion and queries paused with a risk of data loss after a holding period).

OneLake availability for a KQL database can be enabled at either the database level (covering all current and future tables, with optional backfill of existing data) or at the individual table level. The KQL retention policy also governs the OneLake copy: data aged out of the KQL database is concurrently soft-deleted from OneLake.

When OneLake availability is active, an adaptive batching mechanism delays writes to OneLake until enough data accumulates to produce optimally-sized Parquet files (typically 200–256 MB). The default maximum delay is up to 3 hours; it can be lowered to as little as 5 minutes via the mirroring policy, though smaller delays risk producing many small files that degrade downstream query performance.

Enabling OneLake availability exposes KQL table data in Delta Lake format, making it directly queryable by other Fabric engines — including Power BI Direct Lake mode, Warehouse, Lakehouse, and Spark notebooks — without any data movement or copy. There is no additional storage charge for the OneLake copy beyond the standard OneLake storage tier already billed.

While OneLake availability is enabled on a table, certain DDL operations are blocked: renaming the table, changing a column's data type, applying row-level security, and deleting or purging rows. These operations require temporarily disabling OneLake availability; re-enabling it triggers a full historic backfill.

Workspace-level surge protection allows capacity administrators to cap each workspace's share of total CU consumption as a percentage over a rolling 24-hour window. When a workspace breaches its threshold it is automatically blocked from accepting new operations; high-priority workspaces can be designated as mission-critical to exempt them from these rules.

An Eventhouse compute node becomes available within 5 to 10 seconds of a cold start because the engine is fully managed and autoscales; architects should account for this warm-up latency when designing latency-sensitive pipelines that may experience idle periods.
